title: Hetero begins shipping generic lenacapavir for HIV prevention to African markets | HealthCare Middle East & Africa - No.1 Health & Pharma Manufacturing Industry Publication
summary: Hetero is among six generic manufacturers licensed by Gilead to produce and supply lenacapavir across 120 low- and middle-income countries.
thbAction: Use the article as an entry point to pitch THB's commercial visibility layer for territory planning, account prioritization, and next-best-action for pharma leadership teams.
contentHtml:
AFRICA—India’s Hetero has begun shipping generic versions of Gilead Sciences’ long-acting HIV prevention medicine lenacapavir to Zambia, Uganda, and Zimbabwe, targeting an initial supply of 300,000 vials to expand access to HIV prevention across the continent.

Administered twice a year, injectable lenacapavir offers an alternative to daily oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP).

The World Health Organization (WHO) recommended the medicine as an additional HIV prevention option in 2025, following clinical trials that demonstrated its effectiveness in reducing the risk of HIV infection.

Hetero is among six generic manufacturers licensed by Gilead to produce and supply lenacapavir across 120 eligible low- and middle-income countries.

The voluntary licensing agreements are intended to expand manufacturing capacity, increase competition, and improve access to affordable HIV prevention medicines.

Manufacturing capacity and regional expansion

Hetero expects to supply generic oral initiation tablets by January 2027, completing its generic version of the PrEP regimen.

Until then, Gilead will continue supplying the oral tablets required to initiate treatment, subject to country-specific requirements.

The company has an annual production capacity of 15 million vials and says it can increase output to meet demand.

It also plans to extend distribution to 10 additional African countries in early 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and procurement arrangements.

Hetero is separately preparing to introduce the medicine in India, pending regulatory clearance.

Dr Vamsi Krishna Bandi, Managing Director of Hetero Group of Companies, said the launch reflected the company’s efforts to improve access to essential medicines across Africa as it approaches its 30th anniversary on the continent.

He identified generic lenacapavir as an opportunity to expand HIV prevention and reduce new infections.

Funding and procurement partnerships

The rollout builds on Hetero’s September 2025 partnership with the Gates Foundation, which included upfront funding and volume guarantees to accelerate the development and manufacture of affordable generic lenacapavir.

The arrangement also supports the supply of affordable active pharmaceutical ingredients to other generic manufacturers, strengthening the wider production network.

The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis, and Malaria is supporting early procurement through its Expert Review Panel (ERP) mechanism.

 This allows eligible products to be purchased on a time-limited basis while manufacturers pursue full regulatory approval or WHO prequalification.

Hetero’s generic injectable formulation and oral initiation tablets have received an ERP recommendation, enabling procurement through eligible Global Fund channels, subject to national requirements.

In Zimbabwe, the medicine is being procured through the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), using Global Fund financing.

UNDP serves as the principal recipient of the country’s Global Fund-supported HIV programme.

The Global Fund reported that more than 189,000 people across 10 countries had received their first lenacapavir dose by November 2026.

It plans to deliver four times the volume in 2027 compared with 2026, with generic products expected to account for a growing share of supplies.

For African pharmaceutical markets, the expansion introduces additional manufacturing capacity into the supply of long-acting HIV prevention medicines.

However, wider patient access will depend on competitive procurement prices, national regulatory approvals, healthcare financing, and the capacity of health facilities to administer injections twice yearly.

Governments, PEPFAR, the Global Fund, and other health partners are supporting country-led introduction plans to integrate the medicine into existing HIV prevention programmes.
